background.definition: Involuntary rhythmic oscillatory movements, generally kinetic (relating to motion) or postural (when body parts are extended against gravity), most commonly affecting the upper extremities. In the 2018 consensus statement by the International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society, tremor is classified along two axes as shown in . Axis 1 includes clinical characteristics such as history, tremor characteristics, associated signs and laboratory tests and Axis 2 specifies etiology. According to this proposed classification system, essential tremor (ET) is considered a syndrome with multiple etiologies that may fall into the tremor category of “action or rest tremor” or under “focal tremor” (Table 1). The proposed definition of ET requires at least a 3-year history of tremor and excludes isolated head and isolated voice tremors. Patients with additional neurologic signs such as mild memory impairment, impaired tandem gait, and subtle body posturing are classified as "ET plus". However, some researchers argue that the designation ET plus is not justified because it is not based on underlying pathology or an appreciable difference in prognosis, and may represent a more advanced stage of disease.

Worldwide pooled prevalence: 1.33%; increases with age to 5.79% in those over age 64 years. Gender did not influence ET prevalence in this study, but in another study, global prevalence was higher in males (0.36%, 95% CI 0.14-1.03) than in females (0.28%, 95% CI 0.11-0.79).

The prevalence of tremor in a community-dwelling elderly population in Brazil was 17.4%; 7.4% had essential tremor, 5.6% had parkinsonian tremor, 2.8% had enhanced physiological tremor, and 1.6% had tremor due to other causes.
Essential tremor is the most common movement disorder.
Familial forms of ET appear to have a younger age of onset, and older ages of onset are associated with more rapid disease progression.

Patients with essential tremor (ET) have a 4-fold increased risk of Parkinson’s disease (PD). In support of an association between ET and PD, both conditions include overlapping motor and non-motor features, presence of Lewy bodies in the brain (15-24% in patients with ET), and relatively high prevalence of rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (26-43% in patients with ET). In addition, there is both an increased prevalence of PD in patients with longstanding antecedent ET and increased prevalence of ET in family members of patients with PD.
There is an association between dementia and ET.
Patients with ET may also have subclinical cognitive deficits compared with age-matched controls.

Sleep disorders are also reported more often in patients with ET, especially poor sleep quality and daytime somnolence; the meta-analysis performed in this study showed that patients with ET had higher scores in the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale than controls and lower scores than those of patients diagnosed with PD.
Hearing impairment is more common in patients with ET.
Vitamin D deficiency has also been noted in patients with ET and other hyperkinetic movement disorders.
Strong family history (autosomal dominant) in about half, with relative risk of 4.7 in first-degree relatives.
One study found family history to have low sensitivity (43.3%) but relatively high specificity (94.4%) when provided by patients with ET.

No single gene has been identified, but genetic analyses have uncovered approximately 14 loci and 11 genes related to ET, in addition to risk or protective genetic factors. Promising loci include 3q13 (ETM1), 2p22-p25 (ETM2), 6p23 and 11p15.

In a case-control genome-wide association study including 483,054 individuals, five independent genome-wide significant loci were identified, associated with approximately 18% of ET heritability. There was genetic overlap with PD and depression.
Case-control studies suggest environmental association with lead and β-carboline alkaloids. Other potential toxins are under investigation.
Abnormal oscillation within olivocerebellar and thalamocortical loops, especially in the ventral intermediate nucleus (VIM), that leads to thalamic rhythmicity.

Authors of a meta-analysis of whole-brain resting-state functional neuroimaging studies concluded that brain activity in ET is altered in the cerebellum, cerebral motor cortex, and nonmotor cortical regions including the prefrontal cortex and insula.

In a study of 10 patients with ET and 10 healthy controls, functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed extensive deactivations primarily involving the cerebellum, sensory-motor cortex, and basal ganglia in patients with ET when asked to maintain a posture compared to both posture maintenance and simulating tremor in controls.

ET severity is increased with increased visual feedback and associated with an abnormal changes in blood-oxygen level-dependent signal in the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway. These authors suggest that lower visual feedback levels could be provided through computing technology to reduce tremor., although this is untested
Autopsy studies have found Lewy bodies, Bergmann gliosis, and axonal torpedoes in patients with ET, but findings are limited by the small number of subjects.
There also appears to be an abnormality of Purkinje cell biology leading to reduced dendritic spine density and arborization in cerebellar cortical tissue.

Diagnosis is clinical and based on visible bilateral action tremor of the hands and forearms, with involvement of the legs, head, and voice in some patients. Resting tremor can occur late in the course. C
Specific diagnostic criteria such as those of the Consensus Conference of the Movement Disorder Society can be used.C
Diagnostic testing is generally not needed. C

Associated weight loss, heat intolerance, diaphoresis, decreased thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
Associated psychiatric symptoms, mainly postural tremor

Distal tremor, elevated BUN/creatinine, does not respond to β-blockers
Low-frequency, high-amplitude tremor with finger-nose testing

list.listitem: See, for the consensus statement of the Movement Disorder Society on tremor.
Other diagnostic criteria exist, including those of the National Institutes of Health Collaborative Genetic Criteria in 1996 and the Tremor Investigation Group.

Patients with essential tremor (ET) typically present with a bilateral tremor primarily involving the hands and forearms, but it may also involve the head, legs, and voice. Head tremor is present in about one third and is more common in women and leg tremor occurs in about one quarter.
Examination involves careful observation of the tremor. ET is worse with movement and has a frequency of 4 to 12 hertz. Tremor of Parkinson's is at rest and improves with movement.
History features are shown in .

Authors of a systematic review found evidence supporting a familial aggregation of certain disease features including age at onset, disease progression, alcohol responsiveness, parkinsonism and dystonia. The was no evidence of familial clustering for cerebellar signs and action tremor asymmetry.

Drugs that can cause or exacerbate tremor include lithium, antidepressants, bronchodilators, neuroleptics, amiodarone, procainamide, prednisone, cinnarizine, flunarizine, cyclosporin, metoclopramide, methylphenidate, and sodium valproate.
Handwriting is usually of normal size or macrographic with normal pen pressure while in patients with PD, handwriting is micrographic and decrementing with reduced pen pressure.

Numerous tremor rating scales exist, including the WHIGET scale, the scale of Bain and colleagues, as well as a scale developed by the Tremor Research group, although there is no consensus on which one to use. The tremor stability index derived from kinematic measurements from 100 seconds of recording is the newest tool that showed good classification performance for ET and PD.
Consider CBC, electrolytes, BUN, and TSH to rule out anemia, uremia, and hyperthyroidism.
Electrophysiologic tests will reveal abnormal entrainment of motor units at the frequency of tremor (4-12 Hz).
Objective measures such as accelerometers and electromyographic recordings are used mainly in clinical trials.

Transcranial sonographic measures of substantia nigra hyperechogenicity was helpful in differentiating PD from ET in one study, with a sensitivity of 91% and specificity of 91% (LR+ 10, LR- 0.1). Authors of a meta-analysis of 18 studies found a pooled sensitivity and specificity for transcranial sonography for differentiating PD from ET of 85% (95% CI, 79-89%) and 84% (95% CI, 78-88%), respectively.
Use of a magnetic resonance support vector machine may be helpful in distinguishing essential tremor with rest tremor from the tremor of Parkinson disease.
See for a suggested approach to the patient with tremor.
Propranolol and primidone, alone or in combination, are first-line treatments for essential tremor (ET). A
Second-line treatments include other beta-blockers, gabapentin, sotalol, topiramate, and nimodipine. B
Benzodiazepines (e.g., clonazepam and alprazolam) have evidence of benefit, but are limited due to their abuse potential. B
Magnetic resonance imaging-guided ultrasound thalamotomy and deep brain stimulation of the thalamus can be considered in refractory cases. C

The American Academy of Neurology (AAN) recommends propranolol (the only medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration for essential tremor) and primidone, as first-line therapy. Lower-quality evidence supports use of alprazolam and other benzodiazepines, other beta-blockers, gabapentin, topiramate, and nimodipine. The authors noted that the quality of research was limited regarding the effectiveness of pregabalin, zonisamide, or clozapine. For a detailed review of treatment options, see reference 34.

Twelve RCTs have shown that propranolol at doses between 60 and 320 mg/d reduces tremor by 50%. One RCT found long-acting propranolol (Inderal LA) at 80 to 320 mg/d effective and 87% preferred the long-acting formulation due to ease of use. There are limited data on atenolol, but one study suggested it had less effect compared with propranolol. One study on sotalol showed reduced tremor.
Four RCTs of primidone showed reduced limb tremor by 50% at doses between 50 and 1000 mg/d, but treatment was associated with adverse effects such as sedation, nausea, unsteadiness, and confusion.

Authors of a systematic review of 64 treatment trials concluded that propranolol, primidone and topiramate (at doses higher than 200 mg/day) were clinically useful. Alprazolam was classified as possibly useful.
One RCT of gabapentin showed 77% improvement at day 15 as measured by accelerometry.
One RCT found no improvement in ET with pregabalin, with worsening of quality of life score.

In cohort studies, topiramate reduced limb tremor in doses up to 400 mg/d. One double-blind placebo-controlled trial showed 18% to 23% improvement, but with a 40% dropout rate due to side effects. Authors of a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs of topiramate for essential tremor concluded that it was significantly better than placebo with respect to tremor score and severity, motor function and disability, but drop-out rate was significant due to side effects.
Alprazolam reduced tremor by 25% to 34% in 2 studies, but use with caution due to abuse potential.
Clonazepam is of potential benefit as a second-line agent, and clozapine and nimodipine are third-line agents based on AAN guidelines.

The AAN found low-quality evidence supporting use of botulinum toxin, thalamotomy, and deep brain stimulation for ET. Authors of the systematic review of 64 treatment trials, noted above, considered the following as possibly useful - botulinum toxin type A, MRI-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS) thalamotomy, unilateral ventralis intermedius thalamic deep brain stimulation, and radiofrequency thalamotomy.
Botulinum toxin A injection may be effective but is associated with hand weakness. It can be considered for patients who are refractory to medication.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs with 245 participants with tremor found no difference in clinical tremor scale scores for patients with ET between the BoNT-A group and the placebo group.

In another meta-analysis of randomized trials including patients with ET, BoNT significantly reduced both hand and head tremor severity within 6 weeks of treatment (standard mean difference [SMD] -0.58, 95% CI, -0.28 to -0.88, I2 = 0%), but only when using electromyography and not anatomical guidance BoNT injection. Hand weakness did not worsen within 6 weeks of BoNT treatment, as assessed by subjective grip strength.

A randomized trial compared botulinum toxin A injections 12 weeks apart with placebo for essential or isolated head tremor. There was a good response at 6 weeks (NNT = 3) that waned at 12 weeks though.
MRgFUS thalamotomy uses high intensity-focused ultrasound to heat and destroy targeted tissue and is performed under real-time MRI guidance.

The American Society of Stereotactic and Functional Neurosurgery 2020 guideline indications for MRgFUS thalamotomy are a confirmed diagnosis of ET and failure to respond to, intolerance of, or have a medical contraindication to use of at least two medications for ET (1 of which must be a first-line medication), have appendicular tremor that interferes with quality of life, and need unilateral treatment. This recommendation was based on safety and efficacy demonstrated in a single randomized, sham-surgery-controlled RCT and several uncontrolled clinical trials.

In an RCT of 76 patients with refractory ETr, hand-tremor scores, disability and quality of life measures improved more with MRgFUS thalamotomy vs. a sham procedure; results were maintained, with modest loss of efficacy, at 12 months. Adverse events persistent at 12 months in the thalamotomy group included gait disturbance in 9% and paresthesias or numbness in 14%; skull thickness may preclude its use. Skull density ratio (ratio of cortical to cancellous bone) <0.40 is a contraindication.

In a cohort study of 18 patients with ET, 9 with PD, and 3 with ET-PD who underwent MRgFUS thalamotomy, all patients had cessation of tremor in the treated hand immediately following treatment. At 6-24 months follow-up, tremor reappeared in 6 patients (2 with ET, 2 with PD, and 2 with ET-PD) but to a lesser degree than before the procedure in 5. Adverse effects during the procedure included brief vertigo (n = 13), headache (n = 11), dizziness (n = 4), nausea (n = 3), burning scalp sensation (n = 3), vomiting (n = 2) and lip paresthesia (n = 2). Adverse effects lasting after the procedure but resolving by 3 months included gait ataxia (n = 5), unsteady feeling (n = 4), taste disturbances (n = 4), asthenia (n = 4), and hand ataxia (n = 3).

The American Society of Stereotactic and Functional Neurosurgery 2020 guideline notes that early adverse effects, particularly gait disturbance and paresthesias are not uncommon at 36% and 38%, respectively, by one year after treatment, these adverse effects were reduced to 9% and 14%, respectively. Detailed information is provided in this document.

In an observational study of 66 patients undergoing MRgFUS thalamotomy, investigators reported that the degree of benefit on tremor was highly dependent on location and size of lesions with optimal response seen with therapeutic lesions in the posterior portion of the VIM. Among associations observed, adverse effects on speech, gait and dysmetria (lack of coordinated movement) were associated with lesions inferolateral to the thalamus and, for speech, lesions medial to the VIM. Larger lesions increased risk of acute adverse effects.

Authors of a meta-analysis of MRgFUS studies to investigate sustainability of benefit identified 21 articles including 395 patients that reported hand tremor scores. By 36 months post-treatment, there was an 8.8% reduction in treatment effect with time; using time since treatment as a modifier of HTS, there was a a downward trend in effect size that did not reach statistical significance. However, only 4 studies reported outcomes at 24 months or more.

DBS of the thalamus and thalamotomy of the VIM reduce contralateral limb tremor in medically refractory tremor. There are conflicting data regarding the use of DBS for head or voice tremor. DBS, however, compared to thalamotomy, can be reversed by removing the electrodes and leaves little or no residual damage. It should be noted that turning off the stimulator can produce a rebound tremor of greater severity than the original tremor which usually resolves within one hour.

In a follow-up cohort study of 98 patients with tremor or dystonia undergoing DBS of the VIM (61.6% of the original cohort), patients with ET and PD had significant improvement in tremor (mean improvement, 66% and 70%, respectively at 1 year and 48% and 63% beyond 10 years). Forty-eight patients reported minor side effects and two patients suffered serious side effects, one brain hemorrhage and one infection.

Adverse effects from DBS based on a cohort of 728 patients including 144 patients with ET included intraoperative hypotension in 2 (0.3%) and seizure in 2 (0.3%), asymptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) in 4 patients (0.5%), asymptomatic intraventricular hemorrhage in 25 (3.4%), symptomatic ICH in 8 (1.1%), and ischemic infarction in 3 (0.4%).

In one case series of 6 patients with refractory ET undergoing DBS of the posterior subthalamic area, five developed dystonic tics soon after clinical programming which resolved on reducing the electrical stimulation amplitude. Similarly, in another case series of 35 patients with ET, DBS of the caudal zona incerta with unilateral stimulation at increasing amplitudes resulted in deteriorating speech intelligibility in 9 patients. These patients were on average older and had more superior contacts activated during the evaluation.

Authors of a systematic review of 17 papers of DBS found different side effects based on electrode placement. Placement in the thalamus was associated with fatigue while placement in the subthalamic nucleus, based on 3 papers, were mostly followed by affective side effects such as depression or suicide.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 cohort studies including 281 patients with ET undergoing DMS of VIM found a statistically significant improvement in Beck Depression Inventory scores from 12.44 (95% CI 6.63-18.25) preoperatively to 9.18 (95% CI 4.98-13.38) postoperatively.

Authors of a network meta-analysis comparing DMS of VIM vs. PSA identified 19 and 11 studies that met inclusion criteria for short- and long-term follow-up. They found greater short-term tremor reduction with PSA implantation (absolute tremor reduction with PSA -30.94, 95% CI -34.93 to -26.95 vs. Vim -26.26, 95% CI: -33.39 to -19.12], but no difference in long-term efficacy between sites of stimulation. Heterogeneity in scoring systems and lack of transparency in reporting total scores limited direct comparisons across studies.

DBS effects may not be long-lasting. In one follow-up study of 20 patients with ET using DBS, tremor severity worsened over 2 to 10 years. In another study using repeated-measures meta-analysis with 533 patients from 18 primarily retrospective studies, the tremor rating scale total score, hand function subscore and activities of daily living subscore all showed a reduction in the efficacy of DBS improvement over 4 years; the motor subscore, however, remained stable.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 45 papers comparing DBS to MRgFUS, including 1202 patients treated with DBS and 477 treated with MRgFUS thalamotomy, found significantly greater postoperative tremor improvement following bilateral DBS but greater improvement in quality of life following MRgFUS despite higher rates of persistent complications with this modality.
There is insufficient evidence to support the use of gamma knife thalamotomy for the treatment of essential tremor.

Cerebellar low-frequency transcranial magnetic stimulation compared to sham treatment was not effective in reducing tremor in a cross-over trial of 23 patients with ET. In an RCT of 38 patients with ET comparing this treatment to propranolol (90 mg/day after the 10th day), however, both treatments showed similar improvement in Fahn-Tolosa-Marin clinical scale scores at 30 days, although there was no significant difference in functional disability at any point in time following cerebellar stimulation.

Peripheral nerve stimulation of 40 minutes on the wrist of the hand with more severe tremor was somewhat effective in the immediate post-stimulation period in an RCT of 77 patients with ET. Although there was no difference in the primary endpoint of spiral drawing, intervention patients had greater improvement in upper limb TETRAS tremor scores compared to sham and reported greater improvements in ADLs.
Alcohol reduces tremor but is not a recommended treatment due to abuse potential.
Tetrahydrocannabinol and oral cannabis extract appear ineffective for tremor.

Tremor-control devices, primarily orthoses using biomechanical loading and neuromodulation with electrical stimulation or external tremor-cancelation devices, were evaluated in a systematic review including 12 papers. All devices were designed to control tremor of the upper limbs at different anatomical locations and reported attenuation of tremor of 50% to 98% (low certainty evidence).
Dexterity training carried out 3 times per week for 4 weeks in 8 patients with ET resulted in improved fine manual control but had no influence on tremor.
Patients with cognitive impairment and essential tremor are at greater risk of falls; Activities of Balance Confidence (ABC-6) Scale and gait speed were helpful in predicting fall risk.
Tremor amplitude worsens over time if untreated. C However, this author was unable to find information on the natural history of ET, especially among the very old.

It is commonly accepted that ET does not shorten life expectancy, but this is mainly based on a retrospective case-control study of residents in Rochester, Minnesota. In a Spanish three community population study, there was a small increase in mortality (16.4% vs. 13.9%) for patients with ET, with an adjusted RR of 1.45 (95% CI, 1.01-2.08).B

In a study of 211 children with probable essential tremor (ET), the mean age of onset was 9.7 ± 5.6 years; seven children had tremor at birth. About one third had a family history of ET. Bilateral tremor was present in a children and 55% had functional disabilities due to tremor. Progression was seen in 88 children and most children who were treated medically improved.
Tremor in children appears to be more common in boys.
